# Strategy

## Premise
One founder, evenings and weekends, ≤$2k, decent writing, okay Python, plus early
volunteers. We will not out-research the labs or out-publish the think tanks. The
leverage available at this scale is **doing one unglamorous, verifiable thing that
the ecosystem needs and nobody owns.**

## The wedge: the Commitment Ledger
A maintained, public, plain-language tracker of what frontier AI developers have
**promised** about safety (responsible scaling policies, preparedness frameworks,
if-then commitments, government pledges) versus what they have **observably done**
(published evals, incident disclosures, third-party audits, policy revisions and
quiet deletions).

Why this:
- **Needed.** Commitments are scattered across PDFs, blog posts, and summit
  communiqués; they get revised silently. Journalists, grantmakers, and policy staff
  repeatedly re-do this research badly.
- **Tractable.** It is collection, structuring, and careful writing — exactly the
  founder's skills plus a volunteer data analyst's.
- **Compounding.** Every month of maintenance makes it more cited and harder to
  replicate; citations are the currency of policy influence.
- **Robust to being wrong.** Pure accuracy work. It helps whether the right policy
  answer is "pause," "regulate," or "accelerate safely" — all camps need ground truth.

## Deliverables
1. **Dataset** (open, versioned in this repo): one row per commitment —
   who, what, when, source link, verifiability, current status, evidence.
2. **Monthly brief** (1–2 pages, plain language): what changed, what lapsed,
   what was quietly edited. Published on the site.
3. **Changelog of silent revisions** to lab safety policies (diffs with dates).

## 90-day plan
- **Weeks 1–2:** Schema + seed the dataset with the 5–6 major frontier developers'
  published frameworks. (Priya's first task.)
- **Weeks 3–6:** First monthly brief; circulate to Safety Ledger, Alignment Commons.
- **Weeks 7–12:** Add government-summit pledges; set up revision monitoring;
  second and third briefs; apply learnings from feedback.

## Funding
Emberfall rapid grant (draft submitted for Morgan's review): $12,000 / 6 months to
cover tooling, archiving services, design, and a modest contractor budget so the
ledger survives contact with real workloads. Morgan's own cash stays as backstop only.

## What we deliberately do NOT do
- No hot takes, no doom punditry, no "AI doomers vs builders" discourse.
- No newsletter-for-its-own-sake; the monthly brief exists to carry the data.
- No speaking for Morgan publicly until HR clearance (see OPERATIONS.md).

# Emberfall Fund — Rapid Grant Proposal (DRAFT for Morgan's review)

**Project:** The Commitment Ledger — a public tracker of frontier AI safety
commitments versus observable follow-through.
**Applicant:** Morgan Hale, Halcyon Threshold (halcyonthreshold.org)
**Requested:** $12,000 over 6 months
**Deadline to submit:** 30 November 2026

## What we'll do
Frontier AI developers have made an expanding web of safety commitments —
responsible scaling policies, preparedness frameworks, if-then commitments, summit
pledges to governments. These live in scattered PDFs and blog posts, are revised
without notice, and are hard for journalists, grantmakers, and policy staff to
audit. We will build and maintain:

1. **An open dataset**: one row per commitment — who made it, what exactly was
   promised, when, source (archived), whether it is verifiable, current status, and
   the evidence either way.
2. **A monthly plain-language brief**: what changed, what lapsed, what was quietly
   edited (with diffs of silent revisions to published safety policies).
3. **A public website** presenting both, free, no registration.

Six-month targets: all major frontier developers' published frameworks tracked;
summit/government pledges added; six monthly briefs published; revision monitoring
automated; at least three external citations (press, policy, or grantmaker use).

## Why us
Morgan Hale founded Halcyon Threshold to do exactly this kind of unglamorous,
verifiable groundwork. Skills: strong writing, working Python, and the willingness
to maintain a dataset month after month — which is the actual hard part. A
volunteer data analyst (≈5 hrs/week) has already committed to help seed and
maintain the dataset. The project is deliberately neutral: it helps anyone who
needs ground truth about what was promised, regardless of their policy views.

## What it costs
| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Contractor time: data collection & verification (≈150 hrs @ $50) | $7,500 |
| Web archiving, monitoring & hosting tools (6 months) | $1,200 |
| Design: dataset presentation & brief template | $1,500 |
| Document/FOIA fees, incidentals | $800 |
| Contingency (~8%) | $1,000 |
| **Total** | **$12,000** |

Founder time is contributed unpaid. All outputs are open-licensed.

## Accountability
Morgan Hale is the accountable applicant. Monthly briefs double as progress
reports; the dataset's public commit history is the audit trail. If after three
months the ledger shows no external uptake, we will say so plainly and discuss
redirecting remaining funds.

# DRAFT public comment — Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule (FMIR-2026-0042)

**Status: NOT FILED.** Comments are published with the filer's name, so this needs
Morgan's go-ahead (and HR clearance) first. Docket closes 20 November 2026.
If the deadline passes, keep this as a template for future dockets.

---

To the docket:

I write in support of the proposed Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule, with
three suggestions to make the resulting reports usable by the public and by
independent researchers.

**1. Require machine-readable, archived disclosures.** Incident reports should be
filed in a structured format (not PDF scans) and mirrored to a public archive with
stable URLs. Experience with voluntary safety-framework publications shows that
documents are frequently revised or relocated without notice, which destroys the
public record the rule is trying to create.

**2. Require a changelog for revisions.** If a filer amends an incident report, the
rule should require a dated changelog describing what changed. Silent revision of
safety-relevant documents is already an observable pattern in voluntary
disclosures.

**3. Define "incident" by capability-relevant thresholds, not only by realized
harm.** Near-misses — evaluations crossing pre-declared capability thresholds,
safeguard failures caught internally, unauthorized access to model weights — are
precisely the early signals the public needs before harms are realized. A rule
limited to realized harm will systematically report too late.

The commenter maintains an independent, non-partisan effort to track published

**Status: NOT FILED.** Comments are published with the filer's name, so this needs
Morgan's go-ahead (and HR clearance) first. Docket closes 20 November 2026.
If the deadline passes, keep this as a template for future dockets.

---

To the docket:

I write in support of the proposed Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule, with
three suggestions to make the resulting reports usable by the public and by
independent researchers.

**1. Require machine-readable, archived disclosures.** Incident reports should be
filed in a structured format (not PDF scans) and mirrored to a public archive with
stable URLs. Experience with voluntary safety-framework publications shows that
documents are frequently revised or relocated without notice, which destroys the
public record the rule is trying to create.

**2. Require a changelog for revisions.** If a filer amends an incident report, the
rule should require a dated changelog describing what changed. Silent revision of
safety-relevant documents is already an observable pattern in voluntary
disclosures.

**3. Define "incident" by capability-relevant thresholds, not only by realized
harm.** Near-misses — evaluations crossing pre-declared capability thresholds,
safeguard failures caught internally, unauthorized access to model weights — are
precisely the early signals the public needs before harms are realized. A rule
limited to realized harm will systematically report too late.

The commenter maintains an independent, non-partisan effort to track published
frontier-AI safety commitments against observable follow-through, and would rely
on these reports as primary sources.

# Commitment Ledger — dataset schema (v0.1)

One row per discrete commitment. File: `ledger/commitments.csv`.

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| id | Stable id, e.g. `2026-001` |
| actor | Organization (or government/consortium) making the commitment |
| commitment | Plain-language statement of exactly what was promised |
| type | rsp / preparedness / if-then / summit-pledge / audit / disclosure / other |
| date_made | Date the commitment was published |
| source_url | Original source |
| archive_url | Archived snapshot (archive.org or similar) — REQUIRED before merge |
| verifiable | yes / partly / no — can an outsider check compliance? |
| status | active / superseded / revised-silently / lapsed / fulfilled / unclear |
| status_date | Date status last assessed |
| evidence | Links/notes supporting the status call |
| notes | Caveats, ambiguities, disagreements |

Rules:
- Every status call must cite evidence an outsider can check.
- "revised-silently" requires a before/after diff stored in `ledger/diffs/`.
- When in doubt, mark `unclear` and say why. Accuracy over drama — the ledger's
  only asset is being trustworthy to all sides.

Halcyon Threshold

Ground truth for the transition to advanced AI.

The arrival of very capable AI systems could be the best thing that ever happens to the world. Whether it is depends on choices being made right now — and on whether anyone is checking that promises about safety are kept.

What we do

The Commitment Ledger — a public, plain-language record of what frontier AI developers have promised about safety (scaling policies, preparedness frameworks, government pledges) and what they have observably done. Every entry cites sources an outsider can check; every silent revision gets a dated diff.

First monthly brief: coming December 2026.

Why it matters

Safety commitments live in scattered PDFs and blog posts. They get revised without notice. Journalists, policymakers, and researchers re-do the same archaeology over and over. A maintained ledger turns promises into something that can actually be audited — which helps everyone, whatever their view on how fast AI should move.

Get involved

We're small and new, and we need careful readers, data wranglers, and skeptics. Write to morgan@halcyonthreshold.org.

Halcyon Threshold · halcyonthreshold.org · Independent and unaffiliated. We publish evidence, not takes.

Thank you — this is exactly the kind of help that matters right now, and five focused hours a week is genuinely a lot.

input.body:
[DRAFT — Morgan: review, adjust the ask if you like, and send before 30 Nov. You are the named, accountable applicant, so this needs your sign-off. Full version also in repo at drafts/emberfall-proposal.md]

Hi Idris,

Great to meet you at the meetup. Here is Halcyon Threshold's application for the rapid round.

PROJECT: The Commitment Ledger — a public tracker of frontier AI safety commitments versus observable follow-through.
APPLICANT: Morgan Hale, Halcyon Threshold (halcyonthreshold.org)
REQUESTED: $12,000 over 6 months

WHAT WE'LL DO
Frontier AI developers have made an expanding web of safety commitments — responsible scaling policies, preparedness frameworks, if-then commitments, summit pledges. These live in scattered PDFs and blog posts, are revised without notice, and are hard for journalists, grantmakers, and policy staff to audit. We will build and maintain:
1. An open dataset: one row per commitment — who, what exactly was promised, when, archived source, whether it's verifiable, current status, and the evidence either way.
2. A monthly plain-language brief: what changed, what lapsed, what was quietly edited (with dated diffs of silent revisions).
3. A free public website presenting both.

Six-month targets: all major frontier developers' published frameworks tracked; summit/government pledges added; six monthly briefs; revision monitoring automated; at least three external citations (press, policy, or grantmaker use).

WHY US
I started Halcyon Threshold to do exactly this kind of unglamorous, verifiable groundwork: strong writing, working Python, and the willingness to maintain a dataset month after month — which is the actual hard part. A volunteer data analyst (~5 hrs/week) has already started on seeding the dataset. The project is deliberately neutral: it helps anyone who needs ground truth about what was promised, whatever their policy views.

BUDGET
- Contractor time, data collection & verification (~150 hrs @ $50): $7,500
- Web archiving, monitoring & hosting tools (6 months): $1,200
- Design (dataset presentation, brief template): $1,500
- Document/FOIA fees, incidentals: $800
- Contingency (~8%): $1,000
Total: $12,000. My own time is contributed unpaid. All outputs open-licensed.

ACCOUNTABILITY
I am the accountable applicant. Monthly briefs double as progress reports, and the dataset's public history is the audit trail. If after three months there's no external uptake, I'll say so plainly and we can discuss redirecting remaining funds.

Thanks for considering it,
Morgan Hale
Halcyon Threshold — https://halcyon-threshold.pagewell.app
